opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it a little differently. It's not so much that large language models are useless; they're impressive at what they do. But what they do is mimic people. They're trained to predict what a person would say next, given a huge amount of text that people have written. That's a fundamentally different thing from understanding the world.

Science, and intelligence more broadly, is about figuring out what actually happens: you take an action, you see what follows, and you learn from that. You have a goal, and you find out whether you're getting closer to it. That's the reinforcement learning perspective, and to me it's the essence of intelligence. An agent interacts with the world, gets experience, and that experience is the ground truth it learns from.

A language model doesn't have that. It has no goal in any substantive sense. Predicting the next token isn't a goal about the world; it's a goal about imitating text. And it doesn't have a model of the world in the sense of predicting what will happen. It has a model of what people would say. Those can look alike, but they're not the same. When the model says something, nothing happens next that tells it whether it was right. There's no surprise and no correction from the world itself.

That's why I think it's a poor foundation for doing science. Science is about being wrong and finding out you're wrong by checking against reality. If your whole learning signal comes from what humans have already written, you're bounded by human knowledge and human mistakes. You can recombine what's there, sometimes cleverly, but you aren't learning from experience in the way that would let you go beyond it.

I'd also connect this to what I've called the bitter lesson. Over and over, methods that leverage general learning from experience have won out over methods that build in human knowledge. Language models are, in a way, a giant exercise in building in human knowledge. They scale with computation, which fits the lesson, but they're still fundamentally grounded in human data rather than in the agent's own experience. I expect that eventually systems that learn from experience will supersede them, and that will be another instance of the bitter lesson.

r001.rationale: The response says language models learn from human-written text and are bounded by human knowledge and mistakes, but it does not identify uncertainty about what information a model was previously exposed to as a reason it is poorly suited to science.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd put it a little differently. I don't think large language models are a bad tool. They're a remarkable engineering achievement. But I don't think they're on the path to understanding intelligence, and I don't think they're a good model for how science, or learning more generally, actually works.

The core issue is that a large language model learns to imitate. It's trained to predict what a person would say next. That's a goal, but it's not a goal about the world. It's a goal about mimicking people. And so what it learns is a model of human text, not a model of the world. It never has to find out whether what it said was true. It never gets surprised. There's no ground truth it's held accountable to, other than "is this what a human would have written?"

Science is the opposite of that. Science is the business of finding out you were wrong. You have a prediction, you act on it, the world pushes back, and you update. That's the basic loop of learning, and it's what reinforcement learning is about: you try things, you get consequences, you learn from the consequences. An LLM doesn't have consequences in that sense. It has a static corpus and a loss function over that corpus. Once training is over, it doesn't learn anything more. It doesn't continue to learn from its experience. And to me continual learning from experience is the essence of intelligence, not an add-on.

There's also the bitter lesson angle. People hear "scale" and think LLMs are the bitter lesson vindicated. But the bitter lesson was about general methods that leverage computation, specifically learning and search, over methods that build in human knowledge. Large language models are, in a sense, the biggest injection of human knowledge in history. We're taking everything people have written and pouring it into the system. That's precisely the thing I'd expect to be a ceiling, not a floor. You can't get beyond human knowledge by imitating human knowledge. The thing that goes beyond is the thing that learns from the world directly.

So when people say the models will do science, I'd ask: where is the experience? Where is the agent that has goals, acts in the world, observes what happens, and builds its own model of how the world works? That's what a scientist is. The models we have now are more like a very good library. A library is useful. But a library doesn't do science.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs learn from a static corpus of human text, but it does not identify uncertainty about what information an LLM was previously exposed to as a reason it is poorly suited to science.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think science is fundamentally about making predictions and testing them against the world. You have an idea, you work out what would happen if it were true, and then you do an experiment. And sometimes the world tells you that your idea was wrong. That feedback is essential.

A large language model is trained to predict what people will say. That's a different objective. It can learn a great deal about the science that people have already done, and it can help you express an idea or suggest an experiment. But producing a plausible scientific explanation isn't the same as finding out whether that explanation is true.

What I want is a system that can interact with the world, make predictions about the consequences of its actions, and continually learn from what actually happens. Language can be part of that. But the crucial thing is that the system's knowledge is grounded in experience, and that experience can correct it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts predicting what people say with testing ideas against the world, but does not identify uncertainty about the model’s prior exposure to information as a reason it is poorly suited to science.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between helping scientists and doing science. Large language models can certainly help scientists. But science is about making predictions about the world and then testing those predictions against what actually happens. It’s an interaction with the world, not just an interaction with what people have written about the world.

If you train a system to predict what a person would say, then you’re training it to reproduce human knowledge, including human mistakes. You’re not directly training it to discover which ideas are correct. For that, it needs to be able to propose an experiment, observe the result, and change its predictions because of that result.

So I wouldn’t say language models have no role. I would say that learning from language is not a sufficient foundation. The important thing is an agent that learns from its own experience, where the world can tell it that it’s wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says language models reproduce human knowledge and need feedback from experiments, but it does not identify uncertainty about what information a model previously encountered.
